title: Writing a saxophone chorus: Lonesome Nights
summary: Patrick describes the four-part block voicings in Lonesome Nights; Carter says music is hard to put in words.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well, what about the saxophone chorus? Or your development of the saxophone chorus? This is something

that you're widely acknowledged as being a master of -- how would ... maybe it would be easier if we just dealt with some examples, but how would you describe the process and perhaps the style of how, in these days, or perhaps later, you would go about writing a saxophone chorus?
We have a brief transcription here that you might want to consult, from "Lonesome Nights".

Yes, I saw that. I don't know ... what's the difference between writing a saxophone chorus or a brass chorus? Only in a saxophone chorus, you might be a little more daring, you know, putting more notes in to it. Or more ... what?

Well, how could we describe this saxophone chorus? This is "Lonesome Nights" -- this is what? 1933? Just stylistically, or the mechanics of the music. How could you describe what's going on? We're assuming that this transcription bears some reasonable relation to what you actually wrote at the time.

Well, I think the best way it could be described would be by listening to it! But it's very difficult to put music into words, and that's why -- you know, to show someone a technique of writing, that's something different, but to say how to describe music, I don't know, Jim. I'm not good at labeling music, unless it's, you know, sad music, happy music, fast music, slow music, I don't know.
Give me an example of what you think. Well, perhaps we can go at it this way and say, well, how did you go about writing this thing? What did you write first?
Well, I wrote the melody of the song, which was, you know, in half notes. You know ... da, da, da, da, da ... you know, like that.
And then I guess, what would you call? I don't know ... bee, ba doo dee, ba ..
As That's a kind of saxophone variation of that melody.
Beg your pardon?
As That's a kind of a -- perhaps a variation on that?
Yeah, a variation on the melody and chord structure, you know, but I don't know how to describe it with words.
Well, there are a couple things that occur to me here.
All right.
Just, you know, on the ...
Convince me!

Well, I don't know if it's a matter of convincing; I'm just looking for, you know, perhaps a too easy description of the style here. One thing, just looking at the page -- we have 4 saxophones. That's not okay?
That's right. Yes.
I guess that's an easy enough observation to make. And that we have 4 part harmony.
Yes.
And there's no doubling here.
No. Right.
Also, that all the voices move in block chords, parallel rhythm. For the most part, the chords are, as they are formed by the saxaphones alone, are 7th chords.
Uh huh. 7ths or 9ths.
9ths in relation to the bass, though.
Uh huh.
They are in closed position.
Uh huh. Right.
In terms of the spacing.
Right.
Of the chords. Again, in relation to the bass, they're often in first or second inversion.
Yes. Depending on where the melody is.
Or the base.
Or, where the base is, actually, right.
And just one detail of the voicing, if there's often a frequent clash of a major second in these, especially the clash of the 7th of the chord against the tonic
of the chord, the way they voiced here in closed position. So I mean, does that sound like some sort of a general description of what's going on -- at least in this ...
In general.
Okay.

In General, but I don't know what it means! I don't know what it means to the listener ... I guess maybe we're talking for the music student rather than for the listener who probably couldn't care less, other than it's pleasing to the ear.
Okay.
I ... I ... but for the music student, we could go further, if you'd like.
Please comment.

Well, you just said it. I don't know what else to say. I don't quite know what else to add, and I'm talking slowly because I am looking at this as I talk. No, I think you've explained it quite well. Even better than I could.
